problem: The answer reverses the Ricart–Agrawala reply rule. P2's own timestamp 9 is larger, so P2's own request is later; the rule says defer only when your own timestamp is smaller. P2 must reply at once. The given answer ('P2 defers: its own timestamp 9 is larger') also contradicts the chapter's own exam trap 'a larger own timestamp means reply now'.
fix: P2 sends REPLY at once: its own timestamp 9 is larger, so P1's request with 7 is earlier and P2 has no objection. P1 enters first. (P2 waits for its own N−1 replies; it defers only requests whose timestamps are larger than 9.)

problem: 'Ricart–Agrawala removes RELEASE and replies only to older requests' can be read as saying newer requests never receive a reply. In fact a newer request is deferred and gets its reply when the process leaves the CS.
fix: Ricart–Agrawala removes RELEASE: it replies at once to an older request (or whenever it is not requesting), and holds back the reply to a newer request until it leaves the critical section.
